content:
In today's hearing, Apple is challenging the UK government's refusal to publicly confirm whether it has issued a request to access encrypted user data. Here are the details.

A little background

Earlier last year, The Washington Post reported that the UK government had secretly ordered Apple to build a backdoor into all content uploaded by iCloud users worldwide.

The order itself was also subject to strict gag provisions, with Apple even prohibited from publicly confirming or discussing the request.

The UK government has maintained a neither-confirm-nor-deny policy, neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual such orders, and companies that receive such orders are similarly restricted from disclosing that they have received one.

Because of this reportedly existing but officially never-confirmed order, Apple withdrew the option to enable Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK iCloud users.

The reason is that once ADP is enabled, iCloud backups and other iCloud data categories will be protected by end-to-end encryption. Therefore, Apple refused to comply with the UK's backdoor order and simply stopped offering ADP to new UK users, even though the original order was reportedly aimed at users worldwide.

At this stage, the tug-of-war between Apple and the UK government has two fronts: on one hand, Apple is challenging the underlying request to access encrypted data; on the other, it is challenging the gag order prohibiting it from publicly discussing that request.

In April 2025, a judge rejected the UK government's attempt to keep the basic details of Apple's legal challenge secret, ruling that disclosing the existence of the case would not harm national security.

A few months later, under pressure from the White House, the UK government dropped its demand for access to US user data in the secret order. However, the demand did not disappear entirely: the UK subsequently issued a new notice specifically targeting Apple users within the UK.

Fast-forwarding to a few weeks ago, word came out that Apple had filed a second legal challenge against the UK government after the original global order was replaced by a new order targeting UK users.

Which brings us to today's news.

Apple challenges the secrecy arrangements of the order

According to Reuters, Apple today challenged the UK government's continued refusal to confirm or deny the existence of a new "technical capability notice" at a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) in London.

According to Reuters, Apple's lawyers pointed out that the government's secrecy policy prevents the public from having a meaningful open discussion of the case and undermines the principle of open justice.

Quoted from the report:

At Thursday's hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, Ben Jaffey, a lawyer representing the advocacy groups Privacy International and Liberty, said the government's position had become "absurd." He said "the cat is well and truly out of the bag," meaning the relevant information was already public. He pointed out that US politicians and officials had publicly referenced the original notice, while unnamed UK government sources had also confirmed the matter to the media. Both he and Apple's lawyers argued that the UK government's "neither-confirm-nor-deny" policy was an insult to open justice and prevented the public from having a meaningful discussion of the matter.

To be clear, the focus of today's hearing is on the secrecy of the order, not on whether the UK government actually has the legal power to demand access to Apple's encrypted data.

After today's hearing concludes, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal will rule on whether the government can continue to rely on its "neither-confirm-nor-deny" policy in this case. Reuters noted that a formal hearing on Apple's legal challenge to the technical capability notice itself is unlikely to take place before next year.
